Sadu weaving cooperative · Negev & Arabian desert

Woven by hand, read like a story.

Twenty-three Bedouin women weave sheep's wool and goat hair on ground looms, in patterns passed from grandmother to granddaughter. Every piece carries a family's memory.

Order a pieceSee the patterns

Meet the weavers

Spinning, dyeing and weaving take weeks. Each weaver signs her work with a small hidden motif on the back edge.

F

Umm Fatima

Master weaver · 52 yrs

Learned at five. She keeps the cooperative's oldest patterns and teaches every apprentice.

M

Mariam

Dyer · 34 yrs

Gathers madder root and pomegranate rind for the deep reds and golds of our wool.

S

Salha

Spinner · 61 yrs

Spins goat hair into strong black yarn with a hand spindle, as her mother did.

H

Hessa

Apprentice · 19 yrs

The youngest weaver, adding bright modern colorways to traditional geometry.

The patterns

Sadu is a language of geometry. Each motif names something from desert life.

Diamond · Al-Ayn

THE EYE

Protection for the household and travelers against harm.

Zigzag · Al-Marmar

THE PATH

The caravan routes, wadis and the long road home.

Stripes · Al-Khatt

THE LINE

Tent dividers and rugs in rhythmic bands of earth tones.

A craft worth keeping

Founded in 2009, our cooperative pays weavers directly and shares profits equally. Sales fund a school loom room and keep young women rooted in the craft, and in their homeland.

The story of the house

Built by hand, held by three generations

Dar Al-Teen was raised in 1927 by a date farmer and his brothers, who shaped each brick from the soil of their own field and dried it in the Najd sun.

When the family moved to the city, the house sat empty and began to melt back into the ground. Their granddaughter returned in 2018 and rebuilt it with local masons, using the same clay, straw and palm trunks.
